title: The Tea We Make
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 39 of 40
content:
The first cup was too bitter.

The second tasted like someone had peeled an orange into a campfire.

Iroh considered the third with the grave attention of a general reviewing a battlefield.

"I believe," he said, "we have declared war on tea."

"You're the one who told me to keep the smoke-dried peel."

"I said the idea was interesting."

"Those are not the same words."

"No. I may have chosen them carefully."

I laughed.

The kitchen at the Jasmine Dragon was warm from the stove, but rain cooled the window enough for fog to collect along the glass. The morning rush had finished. The staff were eating in the back room, and we had finally claimed an hour to experiment with a blend we could honestly call ours.

Not a famous tea from Iroh's past. Not a magical ingredient from Lanternweald. Something made by two people who liked different flavors and were learning when compromise improved a thing and when it merely diluted it.

On the table lay three jars, a small mortar, a notebook, a receipt, and one sprig of the not-tea vine I'd brought back from a courtyard visit weeks earlier.

Iroh tapped the sprig.

"That plant still refuses to belong in my teapot."

"Not everything green needs to."

"A revolutionary theory."

He smiled, but then he reached for the old recipe card.

I caught the movement.

"We said we'd start without a traditional formula."

"I was only checking the steeping time."

"You're checking the cinnamon ratio."

He looked down.

"Perhaps."

I understood why the card comforted him. It had notes written in a hand I didn't recognize, corrections added over years, and a faint stain at the edge. It carried more than instructions. There were people in its margins.

"I'm not asking you to throw it away," I said.

"I know."

"I just want you to taste what we made before deciding it needs to become something you've already served."

Iroh set the card aside.

"Fair."

We had a practical reason to experiment. The last delivery of fragrant mountain leaves was smaller than expected, and the familiar premium blend would cost too much to serve as the everyday house cup. The staff had asked for a more affordable option that still tasted like something they were proud to pour.

I wanted to solve the problem by adding more citrus.

Iroh wanted to solve it with patience.

Neither was a complete method.

Mina, who had been covering the morning service, came in carrying a tray of empty cups.

"Are you making the kitchen smell like a burned orchard on purpose?" she asked.

Iroh bowed his head.

"We are exploring possibilities."

"Well, the possibilities have escaped under the door."

I covered my mouth.

Mina examined the jars.

"How much does each cup cost?"

Iroh paused.

"That is a very sensible question."

"Someone has to ask it," she said.

We put aside the tasting spoons and worked through the actual ingredients. The dried peel was inexpensive, but preparing it took time. The better base leaves were reliable but had to be ordered before the market day. Honey would make every cup sweeter and considerably more expensive; it would also make the recipe unsuitable for customers who didn't want added sweetener.

"What if we leave sweetening to the person drinking it?" I asked.

Mina looked at me.

"Then I don't have to explain why the house blend suddenly costs twice as much."

"Sold."

"Not yet," Iroh said. "We must first make it drinkable."

Mina laughed and returned to work.

I rewrote the recipe with three columns: flavor, cost, and time. Iroh adjusted the charcoal heat so the kettle warmed more gently. We made two small batches with the same base leaf, adding the smoke-dried peel to one and fresh citrus zest to the other.

He tasted the smoky version.

"Still a little fierce."

"That's one word."

"Would you prefer 'angry'?"

"Accurate."

We reduced the peel and tested again. The next cup was softer. I could taste the tea before the smoke, with a bright citrus note that arrived only after I'd swallowed.

Iroh went quiet.

That was usually a good sign.

"Well?" I asked.

He sipped again.

"Unexpected."

"Good unexpected or terrible unexpected?"

He studied me above the rim.

"Good. A little impertinent. Very much like someone I know."

I smiled.

"Does that person have excellent taste?"

"On occasion."

"Careful. You're going to start sounding affectionate."

He reached across the table and touched my hand.

"I was rather hoping to."

The kitchen seemed suddenly warmer.

I thought about the first times we'd talked openly about romance, about my being ethically non-monogamous and preferring polyamory. I hadn't asked him to become my only home or to pretend his own history was smaller than it was. He had asked for honesty and the freedom to say when a plan made him uneasy. We had both kept asking, even when the answers were inconvenient.

"Can I ask something?" I said.

"Of course."

"When you call this *our* tea, does that mean you want me here every day?"

His expression changed.

"No. It means you helped make it, and your contribution belongs on the label. You have other places you love. I would not turn a jar into a leash."

Relief hit me hard enough that I laughed.

"That was a very specific fear."

"Then I am glad you named it."

We wrote the first label together. My handwriting leaned to the right; his was carefully shaped. The two lines looked terrible beside each other.

"Absolutely dreadful," I said.

"Unique," Iroh corrected.

Mina returned and asked to taste the final batch before we named it. She took a sip, made a thoughtful noise, and asked how long the peel had been dried.

"Long enough that I nearly gave up," I said.

"Then the drying time needs to be on the recipe."

I added it.

She checked the price and nodded.

"I can serve that."

Coming from Mina, the compliment meant more than a poem.

We offered a small sample to the afternoon customers. Halen, who had never trusted a new tea simply because Iroh liked it, asked for an ordinary cup first and compared the two.

"The new one is strange," he said.

"Unpleasantly?" Iroh asked.

"No. Just strange."

He ordered another.

That was an endorsement.

At sunset, we counted the sample cups. We had sold enough to justify a small batch, not enough to pretend the new blend would replace everything else. Iroh wrote the order on the proper sheet, including fair payment for the leaves and enough time for staff preparation.

The first jar sat beside the window.

Both our names were on it.

"What do we call it?" I asked.

He looked at the rain sliding down the glass.

"Something simple."

"Not 'The General's Triumphant Citrus'?"

"An excellent way to frighten customers."

"Then 'After the Rain'?"

He considered.

"'Jasmine After Rain,'" he said.

I smiled.

It sounded like the kind of name a person might remember without having to know the history behind it.

We cleaned the kitchen together. Iroh washed the mortar while I dried the cups. When I tried to take the last heavy pot from him, he looked at me over the rim.

"I am capable of washing one pot."

"I know."

"Then why are you rescuing me?"

I laughed.

"Bad habit."

"Perhaps we could both practice letting the other finish."

We did.

At the end of the evening, with the kitchen finally quiet, he drew me close and asked if I wanted to stay. I kissed him before answering, then pulled back to give the question its proper words.

"Yes. Tonight I do."

He smiled against my cheek.

We turned out the stove, left the first jar labeled in two different hands, and went upstairs.

In the morning, the jar was still there.

So was the recipe, complete with cost, drying time, and the words Mina had added at the bottom:

*Please do not set the kitchen on fire while inventing the next one.*
